extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists interested in the Volkswagen 'Dieselgate' emissions scandal and related regulatory/legal outcomes
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive, encyclopedic overview of the Volkswagen emissions-cheating scandal (commonly 'Dieselgate'), summarizing findings, regulatory actions, litigation, settlements, health impacts, and industry consequences across jurisdictions. The page compiles news reports, official notices, studies and government documents about the scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on 'defeat devices'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Defeat devices' — software or hardware intended to subvert emissions tests — are prohibited; VW installed 'defeat devices' to subvert emissions tests, high court finds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly refers to regulators and courts finding that Volkswagen installed defeat devices. Consequences include Notices of Violation by agencies (EPA), criminal probes, executive charges, fines, recalls, and court rulings against the company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity with emission limits and type approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Vehicles must meet statutory emissions limits (e.g., NOx limits) and retain valid type approval/certification; irregularities or exceedances can trigger inspections and withdrawal of approvals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References include KBA inspections determining nitrogen oxide emissions, Hong Kong and other authorities withdrawing type approval or banning models, and governments running testing programmes to compare lab vs on-road emissions. The EU can verify conformity of cars with emission standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory enforcement via Notices of Violation and agency actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies (EPA, CARB, national environment/transport authorities) can issue Notices of Violation, reject recall plans, order recalls, and pursue enforcement actions against manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on the page: EPA 'Notice of Violation' (18 Sept 2015); CARB/California Air Resources Board rejected VW recall plans; many national authorities opened probes or issued press releases and risk notices. Agencies' actions can escalate to civil and criminal enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer compensation and settlement programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Affected owners may be eligible for compensation via settlement programs (buybacks, cash payments, repairs/fixes); settlements set eligibility and payment formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents the Volkswagen/Audi Diesel Emissions Settlement Program in the US (buybacks, up to ~$10,000 for owners), Canadian settlement exhibits, and other national compensation arrangements. Courts and settlement administrators determine specifics and claim processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil litigation and class/action multidistrict litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Class actions, investor suits, and consolidated litigation may be filed on behalf of consumers, dealers, and investors alleging deception, losses, or other harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited items include dozens of class action suits, investor lawsuits over stock drops, appointment of lead counsel (a 'dream team'), and MDL (multi-district) litigation in the US. Litigation strategies, forum choices, and settlement negotiations all appear in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal investigations, prosecutions, and individual liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecutors and law enforcement (FBI, national prosecutors) can investigate and charge executives and employees for conspiracy, obstruction, fraud, or other crimes arising from emissions cheating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page references criminal probes (e.g., German prosecutors, FBI investigations), arrests, and charges (executive arrests, guilty pleas). Criminal outcomes include indictments, custody, trials, and possible convictions of individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fines, penalties and financial settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators and courts can impose fines and penalties on manufacturers; settlements with governments and plaintiffs can reach multi‑billion dollar amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $1.2 billion German fine, a landmark ~$15.3 billion US settlement, and various national penalties. Financial consequences include direct fines, settlement payments, remediation costs, and reputational/market impacts (stock declines, credit rating downgrades).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recalls, technical fixes, and buybacks as remedial options
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators may require recalls, technical fixes/retrofits, or offer buybacks as remedies for non‑compliant vehicles; regulators may accept or reject proposed remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes VW's recall plans, regulators rejecting some fixes (e.g., CARB rejecting VW 2L recall plan), buybacks of large numbers of 2.0L diesels in the US, and court or agency scrutiny about whether fixes impair cars or are adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type approval withdrawal, sales bans and market restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities can withdraw type approval for specific vehicle models or ban sales/registrations of affected vehicles in their jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances cited include Hong Kong banning sale of some models, immediate withdrawal of type approval for a commercial vehicle model, and suspension of sales in countries where approvals were in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health and environmental impact quantification
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent studies and research measure public health impacts and environmental damage from excess emissions, including estimates of premature deaths and pollution damage valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page references studies estimating excess emissions causing premature deaths (e.g., estimated 59 early deaths in the US from certain sales period; later studies estimating thousands in the UK), and academic valuation of human health damage from the fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triggering wider regulatory reform and testing changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Major scandals can lead to revisions in testing regimes, more stringent on‑road testing, and new powers for agencies to verify conformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: governments publishing findings of national testing programmes, EU changes to verify conformity of cars with emission standards, and calls for evolving emissions regulations following Dieselgate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-wide probe and spillover effects on other manufacturers
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of cheating can prompt investigations into other automakers and reveal systemic certification/measurement issues across the industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page documents multiple subsequent probes, recalls, and settlements involving Renault, Nissan, BMW, Daimler, Subaru, Suzuki, Toyota, Hyundai/Kia, Cummins and others — demonstrating industry spillover and scrutiny beyond VW.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate governance, accountability and investor activism
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate governance failures, board oversight, executive accountability, and investor activism (e.g., campaigns against executive pay) are focal points in assessing corporate response and reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited items include calls for independent probes, investor groups seeking inquiries, campaigns targeting executive pay (TCI), and scholarly analysis on board, ownership, and leadership failures leading to the scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of consumer protection and competition authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer protection agencies (e.g., ACCC) and competition authorities may investigate whether marketing, advertising or representations to consumers were misleading or unfair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page references ACCC updates, FTC lawsuits over advertising of diesel vehicles, and national consumer agency investigations that can lead to enforcement, fines or consumer restitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product certification irregularities and falsified test data
rubrics_metrics.description: Falsifying emissions or fuel economy data, or certification irregularities, are treated as regulatory violations that can lead to inquiries, recalls and penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites instances beyond VW (Toyota unit falsifying data, Subaru admitted manipulated fuel economy/emissions data, other manufacturers admitting to falsified vehicle emission data), illustrating a standard that certification and test data must be accurate and verifiable.
